source.title: GRE Score: Generative Risk Evaluation for Large Language Models
source.authors: Zaitang Li; Pin-Yu Chen; Tsung-Yi Ho

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses model scaling and reports GRE robustness-score comparisons by model size, but it does not test the claim’s held-out cross-entropy laws, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, architecture effects, or fit-dependence. Its GRE scores measure a different construct.
record.gate_note: The reported model-size comparisons concern GRE robustness scores, not held-out pretraining loss. The paper reports no loss-versus-parameters/tokens/compute curves, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation results. The robustness-score comparisons are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces the GRE robustness score and compares 7B and 13B chat models (Llama-2, Vicuna) on it. It reports no pretraining loss, no power-law fits, no extrapolation, no compute allocation, no architecture sweep and no downstream-performance scaling curve. GRE scores measure refusal-based adversarial robustness of fine-tuned chat models, a different construct from what V1–V7 name. It also uses only two size points per family, with confounded fine-tuning. Kaplan et al. is only cited as context.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors report that 13B models generally score higher than 7B models, but not on every model and dimension. They argue that targeted architecture and training changes, not parameter scaling alone, are needed for robustness.
record.recipe_differences: No scaling-law method or original loss measurement is applied; this paper evaluates GRE robustness scores.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relation between model size and GRE score varies by model family and evaluation dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: 13B chat models usually score higher on GRE robustness than the 7B versions, but not always. Llama-2 Fairness: 0.882 vs 0.861. Vicuna Privacy: the 7B scores 0.585 vs 0.523 for the 13B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial-robustness (refusal) scores of aligned chat models do not increase uniformly with parameter count across families and risk dimensions.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2026
record.problems: The model-size comparisons use GRE robustness scores rather than held-out loss, and the paper reports no uncertainty for these comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No additional model-size comparison rows were extracted: other comparisons are described only generally or shown in figures without corresponding numerical values in the text.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits.
No shape or architecture comparisons at fixed size.
No other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task scaling curves or loss-based prediction. Only two size points of refusal-robustness scores.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Kaplan et al. (2020) as supporting a non-uniform size–performance relation, which misdescribes that source. The size comparisons are confounded by different fine-tuning, and no uncertainty is reported. Table 1 lists 14 models, while the text says 8 or 12 models.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy measurements or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No tests of predictions from small runs against much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or estimates of parameter/token scaling with compute.
No controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests of scaling-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task performance predictions from scale or pretraining loss.
No investigation of scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or bends in held-out loss curves.
